title: Babylon's infants and the church's song
english: "I will not use another land like you, O Jerusalem," he says, "nor will I place the unclean on an equal footing with the clean, nor will I consider the profane as comparable to the holy; but even when I am outside your dwelling, your longing will approach me (Ps 136:4, 5). And whenever I might depart from this, all my strength would depart as well." For this reason they also made their prayers while looking toward Jerusalem, and they received the power of their prayers there, according to the prayers of Solomon and the divine promises—just as it is necessary for us to look toward the heavenly Jerusalem (Ps 136:6).

For it is not just for the instrument of words to be vigorous when it is not directed toward what it ought to be. Therefore the blessed men devoted their whole life to the care of hymns, saying, "I will sing to the Lord in my life; I will psalm to my God as long as I exist" (Psalm 145:2 (146:2)) (Ps 103:33). And the city was precious to them because of the worship of God established in it, just as it was said before: "For the sake of the house of my God I sought good things for you" (Psalm 121:9 (122:9)).

For the highest and purest gladness is placed in remembering the holy city. In this way the gladnesses that follow will also be good, just as the Lord introduces the sacred foods to us before the common and bodily ones.

The just thing is what they pray the Babylonians receive, namely what they have done (Ps 137:8). For this is the holy judgment according to the words, "The Lord is known as making judgments; in the works of his hands the sinner was caught" (Psalm 9:17 (9:16)). He declares blessed the one who will be able to do this, through whom God reveals the just judgment and turns plundering back upon those who plundered, and killing back upon those who killed. For the ministry belongs to God, and blessed is the one who ministers to God. But it must also be accompanied by knowledge and one's own deliberate choice. So he does not bless Cyrus, the king of the Persians, who conquered the Babylonians, because Cyrus did not know for whose sake he was receiving the strength against them, nor did he know the God who gave it—"For you did not know me," he says (Isaiah 45:4)—nor did he understand that he was being advanced to power for the release of Israel, as the prophecies through Isaiah have it. Rather, the declaration of blessedness will turn to those who repay Babylon in kind, and upon the one who dashes her infants against the rock and kills them. For truly, the first blessedness was never to have seen Babylon at all, nor to have been in the confusion of her evils. But if someone once found himself in her, having fallen away from better things, he would still be blessed if he should do what he suffered, and should take the Babylonians captive in return, and should lead the very souls of the Babylonians to the fear of God. And if he should not allow their infants to grow up but should crush them against the rock, he would be more blessed than many. You would not be wrong to say that the infants of Babylon are the seeds of wickedness and the beginnings of sins of confusion, which the one who is blessed in these things will be eager to destroy by the saving Word—for the rock was Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4)—so that they do not grow or proceed to deeds.

The restoration of Israel's affairs is laid up for them, as the prophecies say, but the church from all the nations enters in beforehand, leaving a second place for those from Jerusalem who will turn back. So also in the present passage we have just heard of the captivity of the nation and the prayer for the punishment of those who took them captive, and now the song follows, announcing the manifestation of the word of God throughout the whole world. Just as in the prophet Isaiah, while the word beforehand laments over Zion that she became desolate and the holy place became a curse, immediately the knowledge of God among the other nations is proclaimed, according to the words, "I became manifest to those not asking for me; I was found by those not seeking me" (Isaiah 65:1).

orientation: Apollinaris is commenting on Psalm 136 (137), explaining why the psalmist refuses to sing in a foreign land, blesses those who repay Babylon, and then turns to Psalm 137 (138) as the church's thanksgiving from all nations.
